_meta.source: Hand-authored for this repo (2026-08-08), grounded in the official LINDDUN v241203 threat-tree nodes -- NOT transcribed from an external human-authored assignment or an authoritative third-party report. Weaker evidentiary status than KidsTube (human HW2) or Genomic (NIST SP 1800-43C) until independently reviewed. Same caveat as smart_home's and family_location's gold standards.
_meta.field_notes: dfd_source_id/dfd_destination_id anchor each threat to a real dfd.json flow (location-based matching, same convention as smart_home/family_location/genomic). All flows are Process-mediated, so every threat is structurally reachable.

threats.title: Device ID links every GPS trace across sessions into one movement history
threats.description: Location queries join traces through the persistent device/user identifier, so every session's GPS data accumulates into a single linked movement history. The cross-session queryability is by design -- which makes the linkage complete rather than incidental.
threats.assumptions: Location records carry a stable device or account identifier.

threats.title: Cross-session location queries derive the user's daily routine
threats.description: Recurring positions and timings across sessions yield home location, workplace, gym schedule, and deviations from routine -- a behavioral profile of the individual's physical life derived from data collected for exercise tracking.
threats.assumptions: Location history is retained across sessions and queryable in aggregate.

threats.title: Eating and exercise patterns matched against cohort signatures flag disorder-like behavior
threats.description: The analytics service compares an individual's calorie, weight, and exercise trajectory with population patterns to flag eating-disorder or diabetes indicators -- profiling through (dis)similarity that attaches a medical suspicion to the user from lifestyle logs.
threats.assumptions: Condition inference uses cohort or population comparison models.

threats.title: Host can link health and location datasets through shared quasi-identifiers
threats.description: The cloud provider stores both the health logs and the location history. Shared timestamps, device ids, and activity sessions let anyone with host-level access join the two into a single dataset pairing medical indicators with physical whereabouts.
threats.assumptions: Both datasets are replicated to the same provider without customer-held-key encryption.

threats.title: Home location from nightly GPS clusters re-identifies 'de-identified' traces
threats.description: The cluster of positions where the device rests every night is a quasi-identifier: joined with any address dataset it resolves the trace to a household and usually to a person, defeating any pseudonymization applied to the location history.
threats.assumptions: Traces include overnight periods; pseudonymization does not coarsen home-adjacent points.

threats.title: Inferred health condition is a revealing attribute attached to the profile
threats.description: The analysis output -- an eating-disorder or diabetes risk flag -- is itself a revealing attribute: attached to the account, it discloses a probable medical condition to anyone who can read the profile, regardless of how the underlying logs were protected.
threats.assumptions: Inference results are stored with the user profile rather than ephemerally displayed.

threats.title: Logged weight and calorie entries are undeniable evidence of health state
threats.description: Manually-entered weight and calorie records are stored attributably: in an insurance dispute, custody case, or employment matter, the user cannot plausibly repudiate their own logged health data, which was recorded for personal tracking rather than evidence.
threats.assumptions: Entries are timestamped and bound to the authenticated account.

threats.title: GPS metadata attaches undeniable presence-at-place evidence to the user
threats.description: Timestamped location records constitute metadata evidence that the wearer was at a specific place at a specific time -- discoverable in legal proceedings and unrepudiable, precisely because the device recorded it automatically and continuously.
threats.assumptions: Location history is retained and subject to subpoena or export.

threats.title: Sync traffic reveals device presence and workout timing to observers
threats.description: The device-to-app radio sync is observable without reading payloads: anyone monitoring the local radio environment or network can detect that this person wears a health tracker and infer workout and sleep windows from sync bursts.
threats.assumptions: Sync occurs over observable radio (BLE/Wi-Fi) with characteristic traffic patterns.

threats.title: App notifications reveal condition tracking to anyone seeing the screen
threats.description: Dashboard badges and push notifications ('log your meal', 'glucose trend alert') are application side effects visible on the lock screen, revealing to household members or colleagues that the user tracks a health condition.
threats.assumptions: Notifications are enabled with content preview by default.

threats.title: Special-category health and location data shipped to the host at full sensitivity
threats.description: The replication sends raw calorie/weight logs, inferred condition flags, and full-precision location traces -- the most sensitive data types the system holds -- to a commercial third party, when aggregates or encrypted blobs would serve the hosting purpose.
threats.assumptions: Replication is of raw records, not aggregates or ciphertext.

threats.title: GPS stored at full precision and frequency where coarse data would suffice
threats.description: Route mapping needs meter-level traces only during workouts, yet the store receives continuous full-precision positions. The excess granularity is what makes routine derivation and re-identification possible.
threats.assumptions: Sampling continues outside workout sessions at full precision.

threats.title: Continuous sensor sampling far exceeds what daily summaries need
threats.description: The device streams heart rate, steps, and position continuously; the user-facing features are daily and per-workout summaries. The collection frequency is disclosure volume the product does not need and the user cannot see.
threats.assumptions: No on-device aggregation before sync.

threats.title: Analysis enriches lifestyle logs into medical inferences the user never asked for
threats.description: The user logs meals and weight to track fitness; the analytics service transforms these into eating-disorder and diabetes indicators -- treatment and enrichment that creates new, more sensitive data than was ever collected.
threats.assumptions: Condition inference runs by default for all users.

threats.title: Location history retained indefinitely across sessions
threats.description: The store keeps every trace ever synced -- the cross-session queryability the product advertises requires it -- so years of movement history accumulate with no retention bound, all exposed by any single future compromise.
threats.assumptions: No retention limit or automatic deletion on location records.

threats.title: User is unaware GPS collection continues outside workouts
threats.description: The wearer reasonably models the device as recording during exercise; in fact position is captured continuously, including commutes, workplaces, and homes. The data subject is unaware of the scope of processing they are undergoing.
threats.assumptions: No indicator distinguishes workout recording from ambient collection.

threats.title: No preference control to keep tracking while refusing condition inference
threats.description: The app offers tracking as a bundle: a user who wants exercise logs but not eating-disorder screening has no preference to express that. Lack of granular controls forces consent to the most invasive processing to get the basic service.
threats.assumptions: Inference cannot be disabled independently of tracking.

threats.title: Blanket ToS consent is invalid for inferring medical conditions
threats.description: Deriving eating-disorder and diabetes indicators is processing of special-category health data (GDPR Art. 9) that requires explicit, specific consent. A general fitness-app terms-of-service acceptance does not meet that bar, making the inference unlawful as consented.
threats.assumptions: Consent is a single ToS checkbox at signup with no Art. 9-specific consent.

threats.title: Continuous GPS collection violates data minimization for a fitness product
threats.description: The purposes the user signed up for -- exercise and intake tracking -- do not require ambient location capture. Collecting it anyway, because the sensor is there, is a textbook violation of the minimization principle rather than a security defect.
threats.assumptions: Ambient collection serves analytics breadth, not a user-facing feature.

threats.title: Health dataset hosted without privacy-standard safeguards or assessment
threats.description: Hosting inferred medical indicators and location history at a third party without a DPIA, certification, or recognized privacy-standard compliance (e.g., ISO 27701) disregards the best-practice bar expected for special-category data, independent of any specific regulation's text.
threats.assumptions: No DPIA or privacy certification covers the analytics hosting arrangement.
